title: Crossing the Chasm
author: Geoffrey A. Moore
theme: Disruptive technology products stall in a gap between enthusiastic early buyers and the cautious mainstream, and they cross it only by winning one narrow niche completely.
summary: Geoffrey Moore wrote this book for companies selling new high-technology products, especially ones that ask customers to change how they work. He builds on the familiar technology adoption life cycle, which groups buyers into innovators, early adopters, the early majority, the late majority and laggards. Each group adopts for different reasons, and each needs to be approached differently.

Moore's key observation is that the gaps between these groups are not equal. The largest by far lies between the early adopters and the early majority. Early adopters are visionaries who want a breakthrough and will tolerate rough edges to get ahead of rivals. The early majority are pragmatists who want proven, reliable improvements and prefer to buy from the market leader. Pragmatists trust references from other pragmatists, so success with visionaries does not persuade them. Many promising companies fall into this chasm after a strong start.

To cross it, Moore borrows the image of a military landing. A company should pick a single, well-defined target segment, often a specific industry with a pressing problem, and concentrate all its resources on dominating it. Being a big fish in a small pond creates the word of mouth and references that pragmatists need, and it gives a base from which to move into neighbouring segments.

Winning that segment requires the whole product: not just the core technology but every service, integration, partner and support element the customer needs to solve the problem fully. Pragmatists will not assemble these pieces themselves.

Moore also covers positioning, urging firms to define their competition clearly so buyers can understand where the product fits, and to state a simple, credible claim. Finally, he discusses choosing distribution channels and pricing that suit mainstream buyers rather than visionaries.
The lasting lesson is that early enthusiasm is not market acceptance; mainstream success comes from disciplined focus on one niche at a time.
takeaway: Before chasing the whole market, pick one niche, deliver a complete solution for it, and win it decisively.

questions.q: In Moore's model, where does the 'chasm' lie?
options: Between early adopters and the early majority
Between the late majority and laggards
Between the early and late majority
questions.why: Moore argues the largest and most dangerous gap separates visionary early adopters from pragmatic early majority buyers.

questions.q: What type of innovation is the chasm most relevant to?
options: Discontinuous innovations that require buyers to change behaviour
questions.why: The chasm matters most when a product demands new habits or infrastructure from customers.

questions.q: What mainly motivates early adopters, the visionaries?
options: A chance for a breakthrough advantage over competitors
Buying only from the market leader
questions.why: Visionaries seek a dramatic leap ahead and accept risk and imperfections to achieve it.

questions.q: Why do references from visionaries fail to convince pragmatists?
options: Pragmatists trust the experience of other pragmatists with similar needs
questions.why: Pragmatists see visionaries as disruptive risk-takers and look instead to peers who share their caution.

questions.q: What military image does Moore use for crossing the chasm?
options: A focused landing to take one beachhead
questions.why: He compares the strategy to a concentrated invasion that secures one target area before advancing.

questions.q: What should a company do with its target segment when crossing the chasm?
options: Concentrate resources to dominate one narrow niche
Spread effort across as many segments as possible
Wait for the market to come to it
questions.why: Dominating a small segment builds the references and word of mouth that pragmatists require.

questions.q: What is meant by the 'whole product'?
options: Every version the company has released
The core product with no add-ons
Everything the customer needs to fully solve the problem, including services and partners
questions.why: Pragmatists expect a complete solution and will not assemble the missing pieces themselves.

questions.q: Why does Moore advise companies to define their competition clearly?
options: So buyers can understand where the product fits and compare it
questions.why: Pragmatists need a reference frame; without visible competition they cannot judge the product's place.

questions.q: How do pragmatists typically prefer to buy?
options: Only after building the product themselves
From whichever vendor is cheapest regardless of support
questions.why: Leaders attract the partners and support that make a product safe for mainstream buyers.

questions.q: What is the book's central lesson?
options: Marketing should target every buyer at once
Mainstream acceptance comes from disciplined focus on one niche at a time
questions.why: Moore warns that early enthusiasm is not market acceptance and that focused niche wins open the mainstream.
